public_rationale: The original experiments support all three parts: biased LLM suggestions changed reported attitudes, affected participants often failed to recognize the influence, and shifts persisted in the warning conditions. This supports Marcus’s limited claim that these effects can occur.
limitations: The cited version is a preprint.
The experiments measured short-term attitudes in writing tasks using deliberately biased suggestions.
Awareness was assessed through participants’ reports.
Persistence after the tested warnings does not establish that all warnings or safeguards are ineffective.

our_interpretation: This is a claim that these effects can occur, not that every LLM interaction influences every user.
The surrounding discussion identifies biased autocomplete suggestions as the relevant setting.
Warnings need not eliminate the effect. The claim does not require proof that every possible warning is ineffective.
criteria.support_condition: Controlled experiments show attitude changes attributable to LLM suggestions, limited recognition of that influence among affected participants, and attitude changes that persist when participants receive warnings.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Reliable tests overturn the cited findings by showing no attributable attitude change, recognition of influence among affected participants, or elimination of the effect in the warning conditions.

evidence.explanation: Two preregistered experiments involving 2,582 participants found attitude effects from biased autocomplete suggestions; awareness questions indicated that many affected participants did not recognize the influence. Experiment 2 also found significant attitude shifts after warnings before writing or disclosure afterward; the repository dates publication of these findings to March 15, 2024.
